newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela gov't urges Congress to OK aluminum sale.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela gov't urges Congress to OK aluminum sale.

text.p: Venezuelan government officials presented to Congress on Thursday a crucial aluminum company privatization contract, and urged Congress to approve it.

"If these companies are not privatized, they will simply drop out of the market by the year 2000 due to international environmental norms," president of state holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana (CVG) Elias Ynaty told reporters.

Investors view the privatization as a key test of the government's mettle to push through structural reforms. The government hopes to sell the aluminum complex, which includes smelters Alcasa and Venalum, bauxite producer Bauxilum and anode producer Carbonorca, by the second half of the year.

Although expected to meet with stiff congressional opposition, Congress President Cristobal Fernandez Dalo said the contracts would be sent immediately to a bicameral commission, currently also studying the privatization contract of CVG iron company Sidor.

"If the sales aren't approved during Congress's ordinary sessions, there is always the possibility of their approval during extraordinary sessions," Fernandez said. Congress closes its legislative season for the summer in mid-July.

Alberto Poletto, president of the Venezuelan Investment Fund (FIV), the government body in charge of privatization, said the successful bidder for the 70 percent share in the complex would be required to invest $600 million over the short term to upgrade production and another $750 million over the mid-term to boost output on Alcasa's as-yet uncompleted production V Line.
The complex currently produces around 620,000 metric tonnes per year, making it the sixth largest single producer in the world, with a four percent world market share.

Yet while electricity costs -- a key component of aluminum production -- are among the lowest in the world, environmental standards are poor with liabilities estimated at over $100 million, Poletto said.

In addition, the companies are saddled with $1.2 billion of debts and have an estimated consolidated cash flow deficit of $600 million over the next five years, making needed upgrades without foreign investment impossible, Poletto said.
"There are huge risks if the companies are not privatized," Poletto said.
Thirteen companies, grouped in four consortia, have qualified to bid for the companies:
-- Comalc, CRA Ltd-RTZ Corp Plc, Norsk Hydro and Reynolds Metals Co ;
-- Daewoo, Kaiser, Venezuela's Morgado and Dell Aqua.
